Description: SCP-5129 is a frog carved out of jade, measuring 10 centimeters in length and dated to be approximately 1000 years old. When in its inactive state, it displays no anomalous characteristics. Once activated by its intended user (SCP-5129-1), it begins to emit harmless levels of █████████ radiation, and air pressure within a 3 meter sphere drops to 27.50 Hg. SCP-5129-1 then telepathically hears a voice1 which is unanimously described as having a deep, booming quality. In every test to date, this voice has only been reported saying: "DO YOU WISH TO EMERGE?" If SCP-5129-1 declines, then SCP-5129 immediately returns to an inactive state.

Feedback is as follows:

+ Zyn
– Zyn

Proper clinical tone for an SCP write-up

I'm personally going to disagree with this—there are several instances of non-clinical phrasing, immediately from the description:

SCP-5129 is a small frog carved out of jade, dated to be approximately one thousand years old. While inactive, it displays no anomalous characteristics. When activated by its intended user (who shall be referred to as SCP-5129-1), it begins to emit harmless levels of █████████ radiation, and air pressure within a ten foot sphere drops to 27.50 Hg.

  • "Small" is a vague measurement and can vary in visualization between individuals. Better to give an objective measurement of the frog so people can immediately know what size it is beyond "small".
  • Numbers greater than 10 (and all measurements with units) should be written as numbers, not words. "Approximately 1000 years".
  • The second sentence can be removed since it's kind of commonsense?
  • The bit in the parentheses is overly long, and can be shortened to "designated SCP-5129-1".
  • Feet are not metric measurements; meters should be used instead.
  • It's not stated where the spherical effect occurs with relation to the object.

The rest of the article has similarly non-clinical writing. Not a huge deal all things considered, but noticeable enough to break immersion for some readers.

Footnotes
1. This voice always speaks in the first or preferred language of SCP-5129-1

No SCP should be allowed to wander around the containment site.

When something "appears" to do or be something, the implication is it is/does something completely different and the actual thing should be interesting enough to elaborate on somewhere in the article.

I really, really enjoyed this. The weird details like the anomaly not affecting people with severed digits was a good start, I honestly enjoyed the description alone enough to upvote this. While I liked the first interview, I was afraid there was going to become a case of too much extra content bringing down the concise and solid main description, but then the escalation of the effect and the story that was told sucked me in.

I love that it gives enough description of the cult to keep us interested without giving everything away. My only quibble is that I feel the Foundation using D-Class from the area where SCP-3873 came from seems like a serious oversight, but you could fix that by making it so the D-Class was recruited from somewhere else in the USA, maybe with a name change, and it wasn't initially apparent he came from Florida. Also, there's a broken collapsible in the addendum area.

Easy upvote and I really hope this gets the attention it deserves because it is a masterwork of an SCP.

(account deleted)

– hide block

I strongly dislike this.

The subject is Caucasian in descent, possessing blonde hair, blue eyes, and pale skin.

You call the skip the subject and not the anomaly or the object. (I'm seeing that error more and more these days — did we stop trying to enforce that or something?) And I keep trying to figure out why it's so hard to refrain from saying "why did you describe an Aryan" — it's not like people aren't allowed to look like that, lol — so I think it's because "pale skin" is wholly unnecessary when you already specify race.

The whole thing about letting a D-class stay with her was terrifying. I like writing the Foundation as 'the nice side of cold' too but this is too far IMO; the dude's a violent felon. What the hell is the Ethics Committee on in this? The Foundation's job isn't to make sure she's got someone to cuddle with, it's to stop her from hurting people/disrupting normality and keep her safe from herself in the process.

And he ended up hurting her, which just makes their move look dumber from a narrative standpoint regardless of the fact that he did it because he was in the cult. Like, the fact that chances led to him being from the cult just proves that they shouldn't have done it. It's not a good way to introduce the notion of letting someone stay with a skip.

Before security could intervene, Junior Researcher Davis had entered the cell and engaged D-36336 in an attempt to divert his attention from SCP-3873. Agent White discharged his firearm at D-36336, grazing JR Davis's left arm, penetrating D-36336's collarbone, and exiting through the shoulderblade. At which point, D-36336 desisted before being approached, shot again, and killed by Agent White. SCP-3873 was examined by medical staff and treated for minor blunt force trauma.

So was Agent White reprimanded for killing a subject who surrendered? Why was he using lethal force in a containment chamber with only one normal human perpetrator anyway? Even civilian tasers can have a range of 25 feet and this room cannot possibly be that big. The Foundation values lives. Even D-class ones, because they need living human bodies to use. Killing someone like this is a waste of personnel. If his behavior is too shit for anything else, he can be amnesticized and assigned to something that doesn't require interacting with a sapient entity.

SCP-3873: That's it, huh? Just a report? Paperwork? I am a person, doctor! I am a human, just like you!

Dr. Porter pauses.

Dr. Porter: I know, Riley. We all know. There are many more like you. Many more who continue to suffer fates that we wish we could help them out of. But we can't. That's a reality that most of us have come to accept. The multiverse is a cruel place. I'm sorry. We have to get back to work now.

The 'I'm sapient waah'/'we don't care I'm doing my job' skip/employee exchange trope is not unique in general or in this application.

It was concluded that the effect had somehow passed onto him when it was neutralized from the initial SCP-3873 host.

Nothing has been established to indicate that this is a thing that can happen. Dropping it as a surprise at the end just leaves more unanswered questions, and not in a good way.

It has been determined that Dr. Porter contracted the anomaly by sheer chance.

Yeah.

Locating the current host of the anomaly is a Delta-level priority. I have assigned Mobile Task Force Iota-10 to monitor governmental and judicial chatter to locate the current host and place them into containment. We have a whole world to search. We will not make this mistake again.

That's cool, but no focus is put on these elements at all until here. The story is about a girl being miserable while men make her miserable, and then the narrative tries to switch to the wide-scale look at the cult's impact on the world instead. The end result is split focus.

Between these nitpicks and some social issue elements I'll refrain from addressing in depth because they're subjective, this whole thing is just uncomfortable and clashes with my headcanon egregiously.

The biggest problem for me is how contrived it is. There's a bunch of really contrived plotting here (the Foundation being willing to leave 3873 and the D-Class together unsupervised for such a long time, the D-Class being a member of the cult, Porter getting the effect by chance), so much so that I initially thought this was one of those articles where someone in the Foundation is removing information to hide something. If that was the intent, and the researchers are covering something up, then it doesn't really coalesce well enough and seems unmotivated. If that wasn't the intent, then this plotting is just extremely contrived and unbelievable.

So it looks like this article is heading into the deletion range. I know that can often feel baffling or upsetting for a first time writer (trust me, you get used to it!), so please take this feedback as advice on your next SCP! If feedback seems harsh, it’s only because I hate when authors keep making the same mistakes until they give up on the wiki. Keep trying, you’ll get there!

Here are a few pitfalls you fell into:

SCP’s are written in clinical, precise language. This piece reads like prose, when a SCP should read like a formal scientific document. I strongly recommend reading the Clinical Tone Guide. Here are a few examples.

“a small table all the way in the back of the chamber”

“All the way in the back” is a very casual way of describing something. “Small” is imprecise.

“Whatever the wearer believes becomes real, and that's anything. Even accidentally.”

Sentence fragments used for emphasis can work in traditional prose, but are out of place in formal scientific writing.

“SCP-5129 seems to be rather “squared”, as if it was what could only be described as “8-bit”.”

“Seems to be” isn’t a great way to describe a SCP. The fictional reader isn’t interested in what it seems to be, they want to know what it is and what it looks like. If there’s a difference between what it is and what it looks like, that should be clear. Using “rather” is imprecise as well.

Beyond the writing style, the content of the SCP has some more fundamental issues. For one, your containment procedures are pretty overblown. From what I can tell, the glasses are only dangerous if somebody touches them. That makes them about as dangerous as a sample of smallpox or a piece of uranium, which is to say, Safe. Euclid is for objects that are unpredictable and need active containment, whereas this thing is fine as long as you don’t poke it. Lock it in a very secure box and don’t let anybody touch it. If you want to be extremely careful, maybe embed it in a block of plastic first. Bam, done.

There’s no narrative arc or story to this piece. Another commenter addressed this above, but basically, you’ve given us this interesting object that can cause all sorts of mayhem and a few lines of mystery about where it came from, but you haven’t gone anywhere with either premise. It’s all setup, with no conclusion.

Mystery and ambiguity is good, but it should be the sort of thing that leaves the reader asking questions once the story is complete. This piece asks the reader to construct a story purely in their head, but is too vague and open-ended to give us the momentum to get there. The payoff to a story can be a sense of horror or mystery, but it still has to be a payoff.

Hope at least some of this helps. I look forward to reading your next article! The wiki has a pretty high attrition rate, so don’t be too discouraged if it takes a while to get one to stick.
